description: We are three undergraduate students who are enthusiastic about the evolving technology world.
summary: Polyphonic Earth makes NASA Earth data accessible through sound. NASA's Earth Information Center shows our changing planet in striking visualizations, but only to people who can see them, and more than 2.2 billion people live with a vision impairment (WHO). Our web app reads EIC visualization frames in the browser in real time, turns each pixel colour back into the data value it stands for, and plays it as music: warm oceans sing high, city lights ring as bells, lightning drums, and rising CO₂ turns a calm chord tense. A local scene plays eight Azerbaijani cities from west to east with NASA POWER data, one bar per decade, so you hear every city end warmer than it started. Before any music, visitors choose how to explore: "I listen" reads everything aloud and explains each sound before it plays; "I watch" runs a silent map with captions for every note. We measured that the sound tells the truth, and the whole app works with a keyboard, a screen reader and four languages.
details:
What it does Polyphonic Earth is an "Earth Jukebox" in the browser. Five scenes each have their own instrument language:

  • Ocean (ECCO2 sea surface temperature and currents): warm water is a high note, cold water a low one, land a soft knock.
  • Night Lights 2012 → 2023 (VIIRS Black Marble): city lights ring as bells; a Time Machine steps through the years and a "Change" stop plays what grew brighter or darker.
  • Lightning from the Space Station (ISS LIS 2017–2023): every slice with flashes hits a drum; tropical storms boom low.
  • Carbon Dioxide in Motion (DYAMOND GEOS): a calm chord gains tension and beating as CO₂ plumes grow.
  • Azerbaijan, west to east (NASA POWER 1981–2024): eight cities from Nakhchivan to Baku, one bar per decade; a higher note means a city was warmer than in its own 1980s.

How it works Each frame of a NASA visualization is drawn into a hidden canvas (192 × 96 grid). Pixel colours are converted back into data values with the visualization's own colour scale, calibrated against the real NASA frames. A sweep plays the map from west to east in eight slices per bar: the value sets the pitch, the amount of data sets the loudness, and the position sets left or right in stereo. Notes are tuned to quarter-tone maqam scales (Rast and Hijaz) with small data bends, so the data stays musical instead of noisy. Layers (melody, harmony, bass, texture) enter one at a time and can be switched on or off.

Accessibility first

  • Start screen: "I listen" (blind and low-vision visitors), "I watch" (deaf and hard-of-hearing visitors) or "Listen and watch".
  • A "How to listen" guide before each scene's first play. With spoken descriptions on, each reference note is announced first and played after the sentence; the music starts only then and ducks gently under speech.
  • Listen by Touch: move a finger, mouse or the arrow keys over the map to hear the value under it; a live request to the NASA POWER API reads out the measured climate of that point.
  • Sound captions for every note, a silent visual mode, optional vibration on Android, slower playback, mono audio, full keyboard control, screen-reader descriptions, and four languages (English, Azerbaijani, Spanish, Russian).
  • A 60-second tour plays all five scenes for a quick overview.

Does the sound tell the truth? (measured)

  • Mingachevir: 1981–1990 average 14.35 °C, 2015–2024 average 15.71 °C (+1.36 °C).
  • Azerbaijan scene: all eight cities are warmer in the 2020s than in the 1980s (+1.51 to +1.91 °C, average +1.66 °C), and the 2020s notes sit about 21 semitones above the 1980s notes; a warmer city-decade never plays a lower note.
  • Night lights: total detected light grew 69 % from 2012 to 2023 in the NASA frames (relative brightness, not official radiance).
  • Ocean: colours decoded at five known places come out in the right warm-to-cold order in 9 of 10 pairs. Limits are stated in the app: ocean and CO₂ values are positions on the colour scale and come from models; city values are reanalysis for a ~50 km grid cell.

Benefits and what we hope to achieve It opens NASA's Earth visualizations to blind and low-vision people, helps deaf visitors through captions and visuals, and gives every listener a new, emotional way to notice climate change. Next, we want to test it with blind and low-vision listeners in Azerbaijan, offer a museum and planetarium mode, and add more NASA datasets.

Tools HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), Tone.js 14.7.77 for real-time audio, the Web Audio, Canvas, Speech Synthesis and Vibration APIs, the NASA POWER API, GitHub Pages for hosting, ffmpeg and a small Node.js script for audio quality checks.

Team Open Guys AI (Mingachevir, Azerbaijan): Amil Isgandarov (web development), Ali Aliyev (music: composition, music theory and audio formatting; he also composed the theme song), Farid Aliyev (design and web development).
